whatToDo.gentle: Keep the strong structure, but make the language and energy sound like Diego's real concern instead of a borrowed pattern.
whatToDo.direct: Preserve the useful mechanics while rebuilding the delivery around a voice Diego can honestly stand behind.
whatToDo.competitive: Keep the system, kill the replica, and let the room hear the owner again.

whyItMatters.gentle: The perspective shift is that authenticity is not less crafted. It is more believable craft.
whyItMatters.direct: Diego shows that a self-owned voice can make the same message more persuasive because the room trusts the messenger more.
whyItMatters.competitive: The strongest upgrade was not louder energy. It was believable ownership.

questions.prompt: What is Chapter 9's main claim about authenticity?

It matters because good speakers should refuse all outside influence
It matters because authenticity replaces the need for preparation

explanation.direct: Gallo treats originality as part of credibility rather than as a decorative personal preference.

questions.prompt: How does Gallo mainly frame enthusiasm in this chapter?

As real commitment that changes audience response when it feels genuine
As a replacement for clear structure

Rewrite the talk so it keeps the useful structure but sounds like Harper's real expertise and voice

Separate useful technique from borrowed identity and rebuild the speech in his own voice

Assuming a polished borrowed style is just as persuasive as a self-owned one
Assuming speakers should stay inside one topic forever

choices: Skipping structure so the talk feels more natural
Using craft and preparation while still sounding rooted in your own expertise and conviction
Copying successful emotion while changing only the wording

Keep the more borrowed register because audiences always trust prestige language more
Remove all rhetorical choices so the appeal sounds completely casual

Because work presentations should avoid confident delivery

choices: Because authenticity makes every earlier tool unnecessary
Because all the earlier tools work better when a believable speaker is carrying them
Because the book's final lesson is to ignore every outside model completely

coreSkill.gentle: Building a talk from real conviction and real voice instead of a borrowed speaking style.
coreSkill.direct: Using craft without letting the delivery become an imitation of somebody else's identity.
coreSkill.competitive: Keeping the tools while making sure the room still hears the real owner of the message.

plan.gentle: If my work presentation starts sounding like a copied keynote, then I will rewrite the section in language that matches how I actually explain the issue.

plan.competitive: If the room is hearing my model instead of me, then I need to cut the imitation before I add anything else.

plan.gentle: If my school speech sounds more like a famous speaker than like me, then I will keep the method but rebuild the delivery in my own voice.
plan.direct: If a class presentation feels borrowed, then I will separate useful technique from copied identity and revise from there.
plan.competitive: If the model voice shows up in class, then the clone moves go out.

plan.gentle: If a personal or community appeal sounds polished but not believable, then I will rewrite it in language that reflects my real concern.
plan.direct: If a community talk feels imported, then I will keep the useful craft and restore self-owned wording and emphasis.
plan.competitive: If the cause matters, then the room should hear conviction and not costume.

back.direct: Chapter 9 solves the secondhand-voice problem by tying originality to credibility and persuasion.
back.competitive: If the room hears imitation under the polish, trust starts leaking.

front.gentle: How does enthusiasm help in this chapter?

front.competitive: What kind of energy does the room actually believe?

back.gentle: Enthusiasm helps when the audience can feel that the speaker truly cares about the message.

front.competitive: What kind of ground should the speaker actually stand on?

back.competitive: Stand on ground you actually own and the room can feel it.

front.direct: What can be borrowed and what should stay self-owned?

back.competitive: All the tools weaken when the room stops trusting the hand using them.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: Chapter 9 says a talk becomes stronger when the audience feels that the message truly belongs to the speaker delivering it. Authenticity matters because real conviction and real voice build trust more effectively than imitation. The line is to learn from strong speakers without copying their identity or style.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: Gallo closes the book by making originality a persuasion discipline. Authenticity does not reject craft. It asks the speaker to use structure, revision, and technique while still sounding rooted in real expertise, real concern, and a self-owned voice.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: A polished imitation can win attention and still lose trust. Chapter 9 closes hard: keep the tools, drop the borrowed persona, and make the room believe the message belongs to the speaker carrying it.
